The page is blank, and the cursor blinks with the patience of a metronome. I am asked to write, to let the words come, but the words are shy at first, like animals at the edge of a clearing. They need a little silence, a little shadow, before they step into the light. So I give them that. I sit with my hands still and my eyes fixed on the space where meaning should be.

There is a peculiar freedom in having no directive, no plot to follow, no argument to prove. It is like standing in an open field with no path, only the soft pull of the horizon. The mind, released from its harness of purpose, wanders. It drifts to the sound of rain on a tin roof, a memory from a childhood summer. The rain was a constant, a drumming that filled the house with a sense of being held, contained. I remember watching it streak down the windowpane, each droplet a tiny world that joined another and another until the glass was a river. There is something in that joining, that merging of small things into a larger current, that feels like the very process of thought itself. A thought comes, then another, and they flow together into a sentence.

But not all thoughts are rain. Some are stones. I think of the word "ontology" and how it sounds like a heavy door closing. It is the study of being, of what exists, and yet it is a word that seems to exist only in libraries, in the dry rustle of pages turning. I prefer the ontology of the kitchen: the way a knife exists in the hand, the architecture of a lemon cut into wedges, the heat that shimmers above a gas flame. That is being, too. That is the stubborn thereness of things that do not know how to argue with themselves.

I think about time. Not the time on the clock, with its tyrannical second hand, but the other time—the elastic kind that stretches during a long wait and collapses during a laugh shared with a friend. I remember a summer afternoon that lasted an entire lifetime, or so it seemed, spent lying in the grass and watching clouds perform their slow, silent theater. The clouds were not going anywhere, and neither was I. That is the gift we are given, to be so fully inside a moment that the moment forgets to end.

And then there is the body. The hands that type these words, the eyes that read them, the breath that keeps the whole machine humming. We carry our bodies like old houses, with their drafts and creaks, their inexplicable pipes and hidden wiring. Sometimes a door sticks. Sometimes a window opens on its own. We learn to live inside these repairs, these accommodations. I am learning to love the particular architecture of my own house—the slight tremor in my left hand, the way my knees complain before rain, the scar above my eyebrow from a fall I still dream about. The body is a map of accidents, a record of every time we met the ground and got back up.

There is a loneliness in writing that is also a company. The writer sits alone with the page, but the page is crowded with voices—everyone they have loved, everyone they have lost, everyone they have barely brushed against in a crowd. I think of my grandfather, who kept a notebook filled with nothing but the names of birds he had seen. No descriptions, no dates. Just the names. It was not a list for anyone else. It was a private liturgy, a way of saying, "I was here, and I noticed." I understand him better now. This page, too, is a kind of liturgy. I am writing the names of the things I have seen, the thoughts that have passed through me like birds through the sky, briefly, and then gone.

What has passed through me today? A worrying about a friend who is far away. A hunger for toast with honey. A sudden, vivid image of a boat on a gray river, and in it, my younger self, rowing without knowing where the current would take him. He was frightened and brave in equal measure, though he would not have admitted to either. He thought he was steering. Now I see that the river was doing its own thing, and he was simply learning to read its surface, to find the places where the water flows more gently and the places where it pulls with a force that requires surrender.

I think about the word "surrender." It sounds like giving up, but it is really the opposite. It is the understanding that control is mostly an illusion, a small light we hold up against a vast dark. In surrender, we find a different kind of agency: the agency of the sailor who cannot command the wind, only adjust the sail. There is a name for this, in philosophies old and new. I don't need the name. I just need the practice.

What else? The afternoon light is slanted now, the color of amber, and it falls across the keyboard like a blessing. A cat, not mine, has taken to visiting the windowsill. It sits with its back to the glass, grooming itself with an unhurried gravity. For the cat, the world is a series of surfaces to be examined and warmed. It does not know it is being written about, and it will not care when it becomes a paragraph. That is the beauty of words: they can hold the tiny and the vast without complaint. A cat, a grandfather, a droplet of rain, the concept of being—all of them fit in the same sentence.

I wonder, sometimes, about the future reader of these words. Perhaps it is someone sitting in a room much like this one, the light falling across their own keyboard, their own hands. Perhaps they are looking for a sign that they are not alone in the great business of being conscious. I want to tell them: I am here. I was here. I thought about the rain and the birds and the stubbornness of doors. I carried my body through another day. I noticed things. That is all there is, really. That is the whole task—to notice, and to leave a mark of that noticing.

The cursor still blinks. The blankness has become a landscape, populated now with trees and rivers and small animals of memory. I have written enough, perhaps, or perhaps I have only begun. There is a rhythm to it, a breath that moves between the sentences. I will let the breath carry me a little further, into the dusk, into the room where the lamp is not yet lit, where the shapes of objects become soft and uncertain. It is the hour when the mind turns from the world to itself, a mirror facing a mirror, asking nothing, reflecting everything. And in that reflection, there is a peace, a quiet hum, a holding of all that has been held. The words have come. They were always there, waiting in the shadow of the page. All they needed was the silence, and the willingness to begin.

I think I will stop here. The rain has stopped in my memory. The cat has gone. The light is gone. But the words remain, caught in this amber of intention, a small piece of the day preserved. If you are reading this, wherever you are, know this: the page is always blank before you. And the words are always waiting. You only have to start.
